analysis.title: Is The War Premium Gone For Good? Goldman's Commodity Desk Says Oil Options Haven't Got The Memo
key_insights: Brent fell 10% to near $93 on Wednesday after the Democratic midterm sweep, its largest one-day drop since April. Hedge funds sold $6.6 billion of Brent in the week before the vote.

Goldman's London desk says length had been added at the highs on expectations of a post-midterm strike. After US leaders acknowledged the vote was a consequence of the war, the odds of further war were repriced. Systematic funds extended the move as crude and products broke key CTA thresholds.
The physical oil market fell further than futures. Bal-November DFL and prompt CFDs turned negative on Wednesday and then bounced. Certain North Sea grades hit their lowest levels since Covid.

Tanker freight has split in two. Atlantic rates dropped sharply after Suezmax ballasters moved into the US Gulf and West Africa. Routes into Asia stay elevated because of Middle East risk premiums and a congested shuttle system that cuts effective VLCC supply.
The US Gulf to UK-Continent rate (TD25) fell from above $200/ton in October to roughly $70. Middle East Gulf to China (TD3C) is near $250/ton. Both levels are read off the chart and are approximate.

Cheap Atlantic freight keeps barrels flowing into a long Europe, while expensive long-haul freight makes it hard to clear the surplus East. North Sea differentials therefore have to fall further to keep the arbitrage to Asia open.

Oil flat price has repriced the odds of a post-midterm strike but implied vol and call skew have not. Persistent upside buying leaves vol looking rich, and put vols collapsed even as flat price fell, which leaves downside convexity looking cheap.

Goldman's preferred oil options trade is to sell the expensive upside through call spreads and call trees, own the cheap downside through 1x2 put spreads or risk reversals, and avoid outright vol length. European airlines have been hedging mainly through three-ways and fences while producer flow has paused.
Goldman's Robert Quinn flagged that calls were repurchased on Nov 5-6 and that the surface showed some bullish posturing. This is in tension with the London desk's view that call skew is rich.

On TTF the desk wants to add length without catching a falling knife. The bull case: Strait LNG flows are about 30% of pre-escalation levels, even an average winter brings deliverability issues, and European storage fill peaks at its lowest level this decade.
Goldman's tracker shows laden vessel volumes through the Strait at roughly 9.7 mtpa on a four-day average as of Nov 1. November to date is 11% of pre-war, down 22 points from October.

The TTF downside risk is a straight-line drop on any de-escalation and resumption of flows. The desk's base case is flows staying at 30% of pre-war levels, with price dropping on headlines and grinding higher on cold forecasts. Polymarket puts a resumption of general flows by year-end at 10%.

The desk is mostly flat TTF and expresses the view through a Dec 95/100 call spread at 1.25, a 4:1 payout with max loss limited to the premium. The strike sits on the 100-euro mark that TTF crossed less than two weeks ago.
Goldman strategists raised their 1Q27 TTF forecast to €74/MWh from €44 on a 45% probability of a low-LNG winter. Combined with a one-standard-deviation cold winter, TTF could reach nearly €150.

US natural gas faces record-warm weather. October heating degree days were the second lowest in 30 years, November is tracking as the lowest on record, and Q4 could be the most bearish on record. Forecasters give the early sudden stratospheric warming little weight against a super El Niño base state for December.

US supply is adjusting. Lower 48 output averaged 108.1 bcf/d over Sunday-Tuesday, 5.3 bcf/d below the mid-September peak. Further November demand losses are increasingly met by production shut-ins as full storage pushes cash prices to shut-in levels, leaving balances less bearish than the weather implies.

Goldman's US gas trade is to buy the Dec26/Jan27 spread at around -47 cents, targeting -35 cents into expiry. The Dec/Jan spread settled at -50 cents on Tuesday, its widest this close to expiry since 2005. Max loss is unlimited.
Historical support for the spread trade: the five warmest Novembers since 2010 all saw Dec/Jan tighten into final settlement, and it has narrowed from this point in 13 of the past 16 years.

Gold: China is adding modest length but Goldman is not seeing re-engagement from its franchise. The desk's CTA model is close to max short, so the pain trade is likely higher. GLD plus iShares ETF local VWAP is about $4,400, so many holders of the autumn increase in holdings are underwater.

Goldman strategists cut their end-2026 gold forecast to $4,150 and end-2027 to $4,800 (from $5,400) on the Fed's hawkish shift. They call the correction an attractive entry point for long-horizon investors.

Copper: macro accounts are buying puts on expected data-center capex downgrades after the Democratic sweep, while micro accounts cite Chinese tightness as a reason not to be short. The desk's rule is not to be short when China is re-stocking.

The SHFE/LME spot arbitrage spiked to roughly +$570/t and the Chinese spot premium to around ¥2,650/t, both read off the chart. The premium incentivises exports from Long Beach, and Goldman says a staggered US tariff that closes the arb could erode the US stockpile by about December 2028.

Goldman thinks the US needs a tariff stagger allowing about 75k MT per month of Cal27 imports. Otherwise China will slowly erode the US stockpile, since November is probably the last month of US over-import.

The desk remains cautious on adding risk and will look to re-engage in TTF once short-term headline risk passes. Goldman strategists still see Brent at $105 by December and $88 on average in 2027 (from $80), with risks tilted to the upside.

The ZeroHedge author notes the White House confirmed minor strikes on Iranian air defenses on Qeshm Island on Friday night, and the IRGC said three more tankers were ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz. The author would be careful selling the rich calls while owning the cheap puts.

sector_views.rationale: The desk is cautious on adding risk. It prefers selling rich call skew and owning cheap puts over outright vol length. Strategists still forecast Brent at $105 by December.
The desk is mostly flat now but looking to add length on low storage and LNG flows at about 30% of pre-war levels. It wants to avoid catching a falling knife on de-escalation headlines.
Record-warm weather is bearish, but shut-ins are limiting the downside to balances. The desk's trade is a tightening of the Dec/Jan spread rather than an outright view.
Near-term the desk sees CTAs close to max short and limited franchise re-engagement. Strategists cut forecasts but call the correction an attractive entry for long-horizon investors.
Macro accounts buy puts on capex downgrade expectations, but Chinese re-stocking and a spiking SHFE/LME arb argue against being short.

risk_factors: A single strike or tanker incident could reverse the oil repricing and the Atlantic freight discount.
De-escalation and a resumption of Strait flows could send TTF down in a straight line.
Selling rich oil calls leaves upside exposed if the war premium returns.
A very cold winter combined with low LNG could push TTF toward €150.
Warm weather and full storage could keep US gas cash prices at shut-in levels.
A staggered US copper tariff that closes the arb could erode the US stockpile, and China is restocking.
Gold faces near-term headwinds from the Fed's hawkish shift and weak franchise demand.
Strikes on Iranian targets and tanker attacks continue through the weekend.

vol_and_positioning: Oil vols went into the week pricing a post-midterm strike that has not happened. Call skew and vol have not followed flat price lower and look rich, while put vols collapsed and leave downside convexity looking cheap.
Goldman's preferred oil structure sells upside through call spreads and call trees and owns the downside through 1x2 put spreads or risk reversals, avoiding outright vol length.
European airlines have been hedging mainly through three-ways and fences while producer flow has paused.
Goldman's Robert Quinn flagged that calls were repurchased on Nov 5-6.
Systematic funds amplified the oil selloff by breaking key CTA thresholds across crude and products.
Hedge funds sold $6.6 billion of Brent in the week before the vote.

Hedge funds hold record US natural gas shorts, referenced from a separate ZeroHedge piece.
Macro accounts have bought copper puts on data-center capex downgrade expectations.
geopolitical: The Strait of Hormuz remains shut or heavily restricted, with LNG flows at about 30% of pre-escalation levels.
The Democratic midterm sweep was read as a consequence of the war, and Republicans are distancing themselves from it. This cut the odds of a post-midterm strike.
The White House confirmed minor strikes on Iranian air defenses on Qeshm Island on Friday night.

Polymarket puts a resumption of general flows through the Strait by year-end at 10%.

Not everyone at Goldman is bullish near-term (gold strategists cut forecasts versus the desk and Privorotsky's constructive view)

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's Robert Quinn flagged that calls were repurchased on Nov 5-6 and the surface showed some bullish posturing, so the buying may be smart money.
tension_points.bear_case: The London desk says flat price repriced the odds of a strike but call skew and vol did not, so vols have room to compress in a lower realised environment.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A strike that actually materialises would validate the call buying and make selling rich calls costly.

tension_points.bull_case: LNG flows are about 30% of pre-war, storage fill peaks at the lowest level this decade, and strategists see TTF reaching nearly €150 in a cold winter.
tension_points.bear_case: Any de-escalation and resumption of flows would see price move down in a straight line, and the market is well positioned.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A resumption of full Strait flows. Polymarket puts general resumption by year-end at 10%.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's physical data show North Sea differentials at post-Covid lows on cheap Atlantic freight and a long Europe.
tension_points.bear_case: The ZeroHedge author argues the Atlantic glut could vanish the moment one Suezmax decides the Asia arbitrage is worth the trip.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Differentials falling far enough to open the arbitrage to Asia.

tension_points.theme: gold near term versus long term
tension_points.bull_case: The CTA model is close to max short, so the pain trade is likely higher, and strategists call the correction an attractive entry for long-horizon investors.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman's franchise is not re-engaging, the street has drawn twice this year, and the Fed's hawkish shift led to forecast cuts.

theme_stances.key_argument: Flat price repriced the odds of a strike but vol and call skew did not, so rich upside vol can compress while downside puts are cheap.
